title: Sharvari is bringing Indian heritage to the forefront with her Yeh Prem Mol Liya promotional wardrobe
text:
Sharvari Wagh: Redefining Ethnic Glamour in Heirloom Fashion | Style Profile | t2ONLINE

 Goodlife Sharvari is bringing Indian heritage to the forefront with her Yeh Prem Mol Liya promotional wardrobe
 By Zeba Akhtar Ali 
 Published: 21 Nov 2026, 2:54PM | 5 min read .
 Advertisement From her mother’s Patola saree to richly embroidered ensembles by Indian designers, Sharvari’s promotional fashion is a celebration of traditional craftsmanship, heirloom dressing and contemporary Indian style. The actor has been leaning heavily into Indian traditional dressing, showcasing everything from heritage textiles and elaborate embroidery to statement jewellery and silhouettes reimagined for a contemporary audience.
 Rather than a conventional promotional wardrobe dominated by Western gowns and modern separates, her recent appearances have been a celebration of Indian craftsmanship. Patola textiles, zardozi, gota patti, richly embellished lehengas, silk and traditional jewellery have all found a place in her fashion lineup, bringing a distinctly Indian aesthetic to the promotional trail.
 The heirloom Patola saree gets a contemporary makeover 
 One of the most personal looks from the promotional wardrobe is Sharvari’s pink Patola saree, which belonged to her mother. The heirloom was reimagined by ITRH into a contemporary draped skirt, paired with a striking strapless purple corset featuring Jamawar-inspired detailing, zardozi embroidery and elaborate embellishments. The original Patola textile retains its vibrant pink and magenta palette, while the corset introduces a dramatic contrast. The ensemble brings together traditional textile heritage and modern couture construction, with the saree transformed into a silhouette that feels distinctly contemporary.
 The redesign reportedly involved more than 19 hours of craftsmanship, with mirror work, gota, dabka and zardozi embellishments added to the heirloom. The accessories are equally interesting, particularly the crescent-inspired choker featuring intricate metalwork, Meenakari detailing and pearl accents. The look is a reminder that the value of traditional clothing often extends beyond its material and craftsmanship to the memories it carries. Sharvari’s mother gifted her the saree after watching her perform in Jhumka Patola, making the outfit an especially meaningful choice for the film’s promotions.
 Purple and gold by Amaree by Sahib Bhatia 
 The purple ensemble by Amaree by Sahib Bhatia is a masterclass in traditional Indian dressing with a rich, celebratory aesthetic. Featuring intricate embroidery across the neckline, sleeves and hem, the outfit is paired with coordinated striped palazzo pants and a contrasting dupatta. The gold detailing, embroidered borders and ornate motifs lend it a regal quality, while the striped trousers bring an interesting dimension to the otherwise traditional silhouette.
 The ensemble is crafted in Muga silk brocade and features hand embroidery incorporating custom hand-cut gota patti, glass beads, threadwork and sequins. The embroidered palazzo pants and dupatta complete the set, making it a richly detailed festive outfit. Sharvari pairs it with statement blue-and-silver earrings, softly styled open hair and light makeup, allowing the embroidery and colour combination to remain the focal point. The outfit, reportedly priced at ₹1,09,900, is an example of how the classic kurta-palazzo silhouette can be elevated through textile and craftsmanship.
 Soft pink elegance by Jigviva 
 Advertisement 
 Sharvari’s pink ensemble by Jigviva, the label by Jigvijay and Varsha, takes a softer approach to traditional dressing. The flowing silhouette, delicate embroidery and sheer dupatta create a romantic aesthetic that is quite different from the more heavily embellished looks in her promotional wardrobe. The pastel pink palette makes the ensemble feel light and graceful, while the detailed work on the outfit adds a festive element.
 The look embraces a feminine silhouette and delicate detailing rather than overwhelming embellishment. The styling complements the softness of the outfit, allowing the colour, fabric and embroidery to do the talking. It is a reminder that Indian occasion wear need not always rely on heavy colours or maximalist ornamentation to make an impact. Sometimes, softness is the statement.
 Mustard magic by Baise Gaba 
 The mustard lehenga by Baise Gaba brings a distinctly festive mood to Sharvari’s promotional wardrobe. The voluminous skirt features pink detailing and a richly finished border, while the matching blouse has an open-back design and magenta embroidery around the neckline. A sheer mustard dupatta completes the ensemble, adding movement and softness while complementing the fuller skirt.
 The colour combination of mustard and pink is particularly striking, offering a refreshing alternative to the conventional red-and-gold festive palette. Sharvari accessorises the look with layered kundan jewellery, stacked bangles, pink-accented earrings and a maang tikka featuring a green stone. The styling embraces traditional festive glamour while keeping the overall look youthful. For wedding guests and festive dressing enthusiasts, this is perhaps one of the most wearable inspirations from the campaign: a vibrant lehenga, traditional jewellery and a silhouette that feels celebratory without being overly formal.
 A riot of colour in Iqbal Hussain 
 At the trailer launch, Sharvari stepped out in a multicoloured lehenga by Iqbal Hussain, embracing a more maximalist approach to Indian festive fashion. The ensemble brings together shades of pink, green, coral and maroon, with a floral skirt, contrasting blouse and richly bordered dupatta. The pink blouse features intricate floral embroidery, while the voluminous skirt is decorated with colourful motifs and broad mustard-gold panels. The maroon-red dupatta adds another layer of richness to the ensemble.
 Advertisement Her jewellery follows the same maximalist mood, with silver jewellery featuring coloured enamel that picks up the different shades of the lehenga. The result is a celebration of colour, ornamentation and traditional Indian occasionwear. In a fashion moment where minimalism often dominates celebrity dressing, this look makes a case for embracing maximalist Indian fashion with confidence.
 Old-world glamour in Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla 
 Sharvari’s sage-green ensemble by Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla is perhaps the most regal of the looks. The pistachio-green tissue Anarkali belongs to the designers’ Thousand and One Nights collection and features intricate zardozi hand embroidery. The fitted bodice, deep neckline, embellished sleeves and voluminous skirt create a dramatic silhouette, while the matching tissue dupatta, finished with an ornate border, adds to the ensemble’s grandeur.
 Zardozi, a traditional embroidery technique involving metallic threads and embellishments, is one of the designers’ signature crafts. In this ensemble, the intricate embroidery and lustrous tissue fabric create an old-world aesthetic that feels particularly suited to wedding celebrations and formal festive occasions. Sharvari lets the embroidery take centre stage, opting for statement chaandbalis with kaan chains from Surmeyi rather than a necklace. Her half-up, half-down hairstyle and softly defined makeup complete the look without competing with the outfit’s detailing.
 A wardrobe rooted in heritage 
 What makes Sharvari’s Yeh Prem Mol Liya promotional wardrobe interesting is its diversity. There is no single formula for traditional dressing here. An heirloom Patola saree is transformed into couture, a purple kurta-palazzo set embraces rich embroidery, a pink ensemble celebrates soft elegance, and colourful lehengas bring the festive spirit alive.
 Together, these looks underline a larger fashion conversation around Indian heritage dressing. Traditional textiles, regional influences, intricate crafts and heirloom pieces are increasingly being interpreted through contemporary silhouettes, making them relevant to a new generation.
 Sharvari’s wardrobe is not merely about wearing Indian clothes. It is about showcasing the possibilities of Indian fashion, where tradition can be personal, playful, maximalist, modern and deeply rooted in craftsmanship, all at once.
